Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

Key findings  
• 3-day history of frequent watery stools (~6–7/day), intermittent left-sided lower abdominal cramps, initial vomiting now resolved, subjective fever at onset, weakness.  
• Temporal link to restaurant meal 4 days ago.  
• Able to maintain oral fluids; no blood in stool or vomit.  
• No chronic GI disease; only past history is asthma.

Working diagnosis  
• Acute viral gastroenteritis – most consistent with abrupt onset, self-limiting course, mild household transmission (child vomited once), and absence of red-flag features (bloody stool, severe persistent fever, dehydration).

Plan  
• Conservative management: maintain oral hydration; oral rehydration solution (e.g., Dioralyte).  
• Symptomatic relief: paracetamol 1 g (two 500 mg tablets) up to four times daily PRN for fever or discomfort (dose/frequency clarified during consult).  
• Rest and 2–3 days off work advised.  
• Safety-net: if symptoms persist >3–4 days, worsen, or blood appears in stool/vomit, return for review; may require stool culture and further investigations.  
• Review asthma control if any respiratory issues arise (not currently problematic).

Considerations (additional but less likely DDx)  
• Acute bacterial food-borne infection (Salmonella/Campylobacter/ETEC) – medium likelihood; onset after takeaway meal and abdominal cramps but no bloody stool and no widespread household illness.  
• Diverticulitis with secondary diarrhoea – low likelihood; left-sided pain fits but age unspecified and pain not focal/severe.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)

1. Acute viral gastroenteritis – High likelihood; abrupt watery diarrhoea, brief vomiting, subjective fever, mild secondary household illness, usually self-limiting.  
2. Acute bacterial food-borne infection (e.g., Salmonella/Campylobacter/ETEC) – Medium likelihood; onset after takeaway meal, abdominal cramps; lacks blood in stool and household cluster.  
3. Diverticulitis – Low likelihood; left-lower-quadrant pain aligns, but pain is intermittent and overshadowed by high-volume diarrhoea, no systemic inflammatory signs documented.
